How "oldschool" graphics work, part 2 - Apple and Atari

You know I was just reading about how bizarre the Apple 2 handled color graphics. You can actually read the articles Ken Williams (of Sierra Online fame) wrote about them here. I'm under the impression he pioneered the use of them with the early Sierra adventure games.

http://www.cgwmuseum.org/galleries/index.php?year=1981&pub=6&id=1
Another find in there.. review of Ultima.
Yay! I really liked the first video!

It's wackier than shown in the video. Sure, you have the 7 b&w pixel (3.5 color pixel) horizontal groupings. But the order the rows are stored in gets really fun to track. First 40 bytes is row 0. Next 40 bytes is row 64, then next 40 is row 128. Then 8 bytes are unused to get back at a multiple of 128. (Some programs store data in these 8 byte gaps). Then comes rows 8, 72, 136, and another gap, adding 8 after each set of 3 rows until rows 56, 120, and 184 are there and then row 1. The reason it looked like a ventian blinds effect loading images from disk is because of the unusual storage order.

You might think that graphics designers nowadays have it much harder with all the polygons and shaders and whatnot nowadays, but the creation of "oldschool" graphics required a form of ingenuity of its own.
